options: A password the model needs before it can answer
Always exactly one word of text
A chunk of text the model treats as one unit, such as a word, part of a word or a punctuation mark
One letter of the alphabet
questions.explanation: Tokens are chunks of text. Common words are often one token, rare words are split into pieces, and punctuation usually gets tokens of its own.

questions.prompt: What does the model actually work with when it reads your message?
options: A list of token ID numbers
The letters of your message, one by one
A photo of your message
The meaning of each sentence, stored as words
questions.explanation: The tokenizer turns your text into token IDs, numbers that each stand for one token. The model works only with those numbers, and its answer is turned back into text at the end.

questions.prompt: An app lets each answer use up to 400 tokens. Roughly how many English words is that?
options: About 100 words
About 1,600 words
About 400 words
About 300 words
questions.explanation: In English, a token is about three-quarters of a word, so 400 tokens is roughly 300 words. It's a rule of thumb: the exact number depends on the text.

questions.prompt: You build a chatbot that answers in English and in Hindi, using a pay-per-token API. Compared with English, what should you expect for the same answers in Hindi?
options: Exactly the same cost, because the meaning is the same
Usually more tokens, so a higher bill and less room in the context window
Fewer tokens, because Hindi words are shorter
No difference in tokens, but slower typing
questions.explanation: Tokenizers learn mostly from English text, so Hindi is often split into smaller pieces. Our example sentence took 7 tokens in English and 23 in Hindi with GPT-4o's tokenizer.

questions.prompt: What is a model's context window?
options: The window on screen where the chat appears
How many days the model remembers your chats
The most tokens it can work with at once, including the conversation and its own answer
The list of websites it was trained on
questions.explanation: The context window is a limit in tokens. Your question, the conversation so far and the model's answer all have to fit inside it.

questions.prompt: Deep into a very long chat, a chatbot forgets a detail you gave it in your first message. What's the most likely reason?
options: The early part of the chat no longer fits in the context window, so it was dropped or summarised
The chatbot decided the detail wasn't important and deleted it on purpose
Someone at the company removed your message
Chatbots forget everything after ten messages
questions.explanation: The app sends the whole conversation with each new message. Once that's bigger than the context window, the oldest parts have to be dropped or summarised, so details from the start can be lost.

questions.prompt: A chatbot says there are two r's in "strawberry". Which explanation fits best?
options: Its training data spelled strawberry wrongly
It was set to a very high temperature
It ran out of tokens in its context window
It sees tokens like "st", "raw" and "berry", not individual letters
questions.explanation: The model works with token IDs, not letters. To count the r's it has to guess what letters are inside each token, which is why letter-counting questions trip it up.

questions.prompt: How do AI companies usually charge developers for using their models?
options: A fixed fee per question, whatever its length
Per token, with output tokens costing more than input tokens
Per minute that the model spends thinking
Per word in the answer only
questions.explanation: Prices are quoted per million tokens, with separate prices for input and output. Output usually costs more: Anthropic, for example, charges five times as much per output token.
